sections.overview: Amphimedon queenslandica is a marine demosponge in the family Niphatidae, described from Heron and One Tree islands on Australia’s southern Great Barrier Reef. It became a prominent research species after its genome was sequenced.
sections.identification: Its body grows as a blue-green encrusting base with rounded, lobed or finger-like projections. Large openings sit on raised tips; the outer surface is smooth and translucent, with spongin-rich fibres and small, slightly curved siliceous spicules. A French natural-history guide reports 7–15 cm, without defining the measurement. A Heron Island study instead measured adults at about 1–112 cm² of surface area, not standard length, height or mass.
sections.habitat: It attaches to hard material such as coral rubble and rock on shallow reef flats and crests. On the southern Great Barrier Reef it occurs patchily, often beneath boulders or in crevices and sandy gaps, especially where water flow is low.
sections.diet: It filters microbes and particulate organic matter from seawater drawn through pores and internal chambers by flagellated collar cells, a suspension-feeding system typical of sponges.
sections.behavior: Adults attach to hard surfaces and remain in place, pumping water through a porous network of chambers and canals. Their dynamic tissues can remodel the body, while internal flow supplies food and oxygen and removes waste.
sections.reproduction: Individuals are simultaneous hermaphrodites: they release sperm into seawater but retain eggs and embryos in brood chambers. Larvae are released throughout the year; after a planktonic phase they settle and metamorphose when they become responsive to reef signals.
sections.ecology: Adult sponges host commensal microbes, and one bacterial genome was recovered alongside the sponge genome project. The species is also a model for studying animal origins because its genome preserves many cell-signalling and developmental genes shared across animals.
sections.conservation: At studied southern Great Barrier Reef sites it is locally common but patchily distributed; these records do not estimate abundance across its full range.
